speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for your cooperation. To begin our assessment, could you please tell me how many days old your baby is, and when you first noticed the yellowish discoloration?

speaker: Patient
text: 5-day-old male newborn. The newborn's mother reports that her child has developed yellowish discoloration of the skin that started from the face and then spread to the trunk since the past day. There have been no changes in his bowel habits or urination. The baby was born full-term at 38 weeks’ gestation via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been exclusively breastfed every 2–3 hours.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Has the baby passed meconium stool, and has it turned green or yellow in the last 48 hours? Also, could you tell me if the stools have been tarry (black) or pale/clay-colored?

REQUEST TEST: Serum bilirubin level (Total and Direct)

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Yellowish discoloration of the skin. I also have Discoloration started from the face then spread to the trunk, Scleral icterus noted. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That diagnosis is highly unlikely for a 5-day-old infant; acute appendicitis is extremely rare in newborns and does not present with generalized jaundice. Can you tell me if the baby is feeding well and gaining weight, or if he has had any episodes of vomiting or fever? Please confirm if you have the laboratory results for the serum bilirubin level we requested.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Born full term at 38 weeks via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. No past medical history. Social history: Exclusive breastfeeding every 2–3 hours.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Physiological Jaundice of the Newborn. The clinical picture of a 5-day-old, full-term infant with progressive jaundice starting on the face and spreading to the trunk, in the absence of poor feeding, vomiting, or fever, is classic for physiological jaundice. The recent referral for "acute appendicitis" was an error, as that condition does not present with generalized skin and scleral yellowing in a newborn.
